Scope warning. This paper evaluates a proposed anatomical severity representation and its use in retrospective / registry-based prediction. It does not establish prospective EMS usability, interrater reliability, time burden, clinical utility, patient benefit, or safe deployment of an AI triage system.

One-page synthesis

Core thesis: PHISE is an imaging-independent anatomical injury score intended for scene use. The study shows that a simplified 8-region score can retain useful information about injury burden and can contribute to ML prediction when paired with prehospital physiology and mechanism data. The strongest evidence is for feasibility and transfusion-risk signal; the evidence is substantially weaker for literal equivalence to ISS/NISS or for real-world prehospital deployment.

What the authors report. In 397,864 NTDB® patients, frequency-weighted LLM classification suggested that 57.06% of injuries could be approximated from clinical/scene knowledge, 39.04% required imaging, and 3.87% were undetermined. The retrospectively constructed PHISE correlated with ISS (ρ=0.61) and especially NISS (ρ=0.79). As a stand-alone score, however, mortality discrimination was lower than ISS/NISS (AUC 0.71 vs 0.83/0.82); transfusion discrimination was closer (0.77 vs 0.83/0.81).

External registry validation included 14,136 patients from Germany, Switzerland and Austria. The paper reports weaker structural agreement (ρ≈0.44 vs ISS and ρ≈0.42 vs NISS). The results text reports markedly lower mortality prediction by PHISE (AUC 0.63; AUPRC 0.19) than ISS/NISS (AUC 0.81/0.84; AUPRC 0.41/0.52), while transfusion prediction was much closer (AUC 0.76 vs 0.78/0.77; AUPRC 0.26 vs 0.31/0.26).

Embedding PHISE in XGBoost with prehospital variables narrows—but does not eliminate—the gap. Figure 5 shows mortality ROC AUC 0.90 vs 0.95 and PR AUC 0.58 vs 0.76 for PHISE- versus ISS-based models; transfusion ROC AUC 0.82 vs 0.88 and PR AUC 0.40 vs 0.53. These differences are clinically and methodologically nontrivial, especially on precision-recall metrics.

Most important interpretive limitation. The NTDB® “PHISE” is not a score collected by paramedics at the scene. Definitive AIS-coded injury descriptions are first used to determine the true injury identity; clinically assessable injuries then inherit severity through AIS→PHISE remapping, while imaging-dependent/undetermined injuries receive randomized severity. This is a simulation of prehospital uncertainty rather than a direct test of prehospital recognition. External registry data partly mitigate this limitation, but the registry uses a pre-existing simplified prehospital injury assessment described as compatible with PHISE, not necessarily the exact prospectively implemented PHISE instrument.
Best-supported use of the paper. A design reference for structured prehospital anatomical features in AI-assisted trauma triage, and a hypothesis-generating justification for prospective EMS validation—not a deployment-ready trauma score.

Section condensation

Background / rationale

ISS and NISS remain standard anatomical trauma-severity measures but depend on definitive anatomical coding and commonly on CT or other imaging, so they are unavailable at the time when field triage, destination selection, trauma-team mobilization and early resource decisions are made. The authors propose PHISE as a deliberately coarse anatomical component that can be assessed from examination, mechanism and scene information, and then combined with physiology rather than treated as a comprehensive risk score.

The paper’s hypothesis is not that PHISE should replace ISS/NISS for definitive injury characterization, but that an earlier approximation may preserve enough signal to support prehospital decision models. The manuscript frames AI/ML as the context in which a lower-information anatomical score may become useful because other prehospital variables can compensate for missing imaging-derived detail.

Results — injury characteristics and imaging requirements

For the 50 most frequent NTDB® injury codes, the authors used LLM-assisted classification to decide whether each injury could be approximated from clinical/scene knowledge, required imaging, or was undetermined. Across the entire AIS dictionary the figure shows 33.90% clinically approximable, 60.88% imaging-dependent and 5.21% undetermined; when weighted by NTDB® injury frequency the distribution reverses to 57.06% clinically approximable, 39.04% imaging-dependent and 3.87% undetermined. External/superficial injuries were least imaging-dependent; head and abdominal/pelvic injuries were most dependent on imaging.

This supports a practical premise—that common injuries are often at least partly scene-assessable—but the classification itself is a model judgment based on AIS descriptions, not observed EMS diagnostic accuracy.

Results — cohort derivation and PHISE structure

The NTDB® flow begins with 1,097,190 patients and yields 397,864 derivation patients after exclusions. The external TraumaRegister DGU® flow begins with 17,144 records from eight university trauma centers and yields 14,136 eligible patients. Severe trauma was much more common in the external cohort (54.4% with ISS>15 vs 21.8% in NTDB®), and the external cohort also had higher ISS/NISS/PHISE distributions and higher reported mortality/transfusion burden.

PHISE expands anatomical categorization from six ISS regions to eight practical regions: head, face/neck, thorax/chest, abdomen, pelvis, upper extremity, lower extremity and spine. Severity is compressed to 0 none, 1 minor, 2 moderate and 3 severe. AIS 0→0, AIS 1→1, AIS 2–3→2 and AIS 4–6→3.

Results — retrospective PHISE derivation and concordance

A standardized LLM prompt was reportedly run three times per input, with majority voting for disagreements and manual spot-checking for face validity. Clinically assessable injuries were mapped from AIS severity to PHISE severity; imaging-dependent or undetermined injuries were randomly assigned severity to simulate prehospital uncertainty. NLP rules mapped AIS body-region descriptions into PHISE regions. Composite PHISE was the sum of squares of the three highest regional PHISE grades.

In NTDB®, PHISE correlated with ISS (ρ=0.6108) and NISS (ρ=0.7882) and had low bin-level calibration Brier values against these scores (0.0270 and 0.0257). The strongest agreement occurred in easily visible injuries and the largest discrepancies in head and abdominal/pelvic regions. Low-severity injuries tended to be overestimated.

Results — stand-alone outcome prediction

In the derivation cohort, mortality ROC AUC was 0.71 for PHISE versus 0.83 for ISS and 0.82 for NISS; mortality AUPRC was approximately 0.11 for PHISE versus 0.26 and 0.32. For RBCC transfusion, PHISE performed closer to the imaging-based scores: ROC AUC 0.77 versus 0.83/0.81, with AUPRC approximately 0.23 versus 0.33/0.25.

In external validation, the results text reports PHISE-vs-ISS/NISS mortality AUC 0.63 vs 0.81/0.84 and AUPRC 0.19 vs 0.41/0.52; transfusion AUC 0.76 vs 0.78/0.77 and AUPRC 0.26 vs 0.31/0.26. Correlation with ISS/NISS fell to about 0.44/0.42, demonstrating a notable loss of structural agreement outside the synthetic derivation setting.

Results — machine-learning integration

XGBoost models incorporated a severity input (PHISE, ISS or NISS) with prehospital variables such as age, sex, GCS, injury mechanism and vital signs. Figure 5 shows that additional prehospital context reduces the performance gap, but the PHISE model remains lower on both ROC and precision-recall discrimination: mortality ROC AUC 0.90 vs 0.95 and PR AUC 0.58 vs 0.76; transfusion ROC AUC 0.82 vs 0.88 and PR AUC 0.40 vs 0.53. SHAP profiles indicate the PHISE model relies more heavily on the accompanying physiologic/clinical variables, consistent with complementarity rather than equivalence of the anatomical score itself.

The text also reports supplementary benchmarking against RISC2, TASH, TRISS and rSIG: RISC2 reportedly reached mortality AUC 0.95 and TASH transfusion AUC 0.88; PHISE-based ML reportedly outperformed rSIG and TRISS. Because Supplementary Fig. S5 and Tables 1–2 were not present in the uploaded source, those comparisons cannot be fully audited here.

Discussion / authors’ interpretation

The authors interpret PHISE as the missing anatomical component for prehospital risk modeling: simpler than ISS/NISS, available without diagnostic imaging, and potentially suitable for AI-enhanced dispatch, transfusion protocols, destination decisions, direct-to-OR routing and ICU planning. They explicitly state that PHISE is not a comprehensive patient-centered risk score and cannot capture physiology, frailty, comorbidity or the full impact of severe isolated brain/spinal injury.

They acknowledge dependence on examiner experience and documentation quality, possible missed occult injuries, and the absence of prospective testing of operationality, interrater reliability, time burden, workflow integration and clinical impact. Those limitations are decisive: the paper is best viewed as model-development evidence rather than validation of a field-ready instrument.

Methods & model architecture

Derivation data
NTDB® 2019
  • Voluntary US trauma registry; >700 hospitals, predominantly Level I/II centers.
  • Only primary admissions included.
  • Starting population 1,097,190; analytic derivation cohort 397,864.
  • Temporal stress test reportedly repeated in NTDB® 2020.
External data
TraumaRegister DGU®
  • Germany, Switzerland and Austria.
  • Six German, one Austrian and one Swiss university trauma center.
  • 17,144 source records → 14,136 eligible.
  • Prehospital simplified injury scoring judged compatible with PHISE logic.

PHISE derivation algorithm

Input: definitive AIS-coded injury descriptions + AIS body-region codes

1. LLM classifies each injury description:
   A. clinically/scene assessable
   B. imaging required
   C. undetermined
2. Run classification three times; majority vote if outputs differ.
3. NLP maps AIS-coded body parts → PHISE anatomical region.
4. Severity assignment:
   - assessable injury: AIS 0→PHISE 0; AIS 1→1; AIS 2–3→2; AIS 4–6→3
   - imaging-required / undetermined: randomized PHISE severity
5. Aggregate patient score:
   PHISE = square of highest regional grade
         + square of second-highest regional grade
         + square of third-highest regional grade
   Maximum = 3² + 3² + 3² = 27.
Construct-validity concern: the derivation uses definitive AIS injury identities to create a simulated prehospital score. Therefore it does not measure whether EMS personnel can correctly detect the injury in the first place; it mainly models what would happen after an injury has been labeled as scene-assessable versus imaging-dependent.

Supervised ML workflow

Derivation cohort
→ random 80/20 training/validation split
→ missing-value imputation (mean continuous / median ordinal / mode categorical)
→ ColumnTransformer scaling
→ multiple candidate classifiers tested
→ XGBoost selected
→ hyperparameter tuning + nested / 10-fold cross-validation
→ internal validation and bootstrap classification metrics
→ SHAP feature importance

Separate multivariable analysis described later:
NTDB® training → TR-DGU® testing
with severity input (PHISE or ISS/NISS) + age + sex + GCS + mechanism + vital signs.

The manuscript describes both internal 80/20 validation and cross-registry testing. Figure 5 does not state the evaluation cohort in its caption, which makes the exact mapping from the methods description to the displayed model metrics less transparent than desirable.

Outcomes and analysis

  • Primary: in-hospital mortality.
  • Secondary: RBCC transfusion need, hospital LOS, ICU LOS.
  • Correlation: Spearman rank correlation.
  • Score calibration: patient-bin averages; 1,000-patient bins in NTDB® and 100-patient bins in TR-DGU® figures.
  • Binary discrimination: ROC and PR analyses; DeLong tests stated for AUC comparisons.
  • ML metrics: sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, F1; 1,000-fold bootstrap; SHAP for feature interpretation.

Figure 4 — external validation

Figure/text conflict. The Results text gives external mortality AUCs PHISE 0.63, ISS 0.81, NISS 0.84, but the legend printed inside Figure 4H shows 0.76, 0.78 and 0.77—the same values shown for the transfusion ROC panel. The mortality curve visually aligns with the poorer PHISE performance described in the text. For appraisal, the Results-text mortality metrics are treated as the intended values, while the figure legend is flagged as a likely labeling/copy error. Figure 4 uses N=13,971 in the correlation panels despite an eligible cohort of 14,136; the reason for this reduction is not stated in the figure.

Title-claim nuance. “Matches” should not be read as statistical equivalence or noninferiority. Figure 5 retains visible discrimination and calibration differences, particularly in precision-recall performance. No equivalence/noninferiority margin is reported.
Additional figure-label issue. Panel D is captioned as mortality calibration but the displayed x-axis reads “Predicted transfusion probability,” suggesting another labeling/copy error. This does not invalidate the entire analysis, but it reduces confidence in figure-level QA and makes supplementary/source-code access more important.

Evaluation & appraisal

Verdict: Read soon. The paper is conceptually useful and directly relevant to prehospital AI/clinical-informatics design, but it should be read as a development/feasibility study rather than evidence that PHISE is ready for clinical use or truly equivalent to ISS/NISS.
Relevance
8/10

Rationale: Directly addresses structured clinical features, early prediction and AI-assisted decision support in a high-stakes domain.

Evidence basis: Two large trauma registries, explicit ML integration, clinically meaningful mortality/transfusion outcomes.
Limiting factor: Focus is trauma/EMS rather than general clinical prediction.
Would raise: Prospective operational study with actionable triage endpoints.

Novelty
8/10

Rationale: The eight-region imaging-independent anatomical score and explicit integration into ML are a useful reframing of prehospital severity representation.

Evidence basis: New PHISE construct, synthetic derivation and cross-registry comparison.
Limiting factor: Simplified prehospital injury scoring and condensed AIS approaches predate this work.
Would raise: Demonstration that PHISE changes care or enables a capability unavailable to existing field scores.

Method strength
6/10

Rationale: Large datasets, external registry testing, calibration, ROC/PR, bootstrap methods and model comparison are strengths; the central score derivation is nevertheless synthetic.

Evidence basis: NTDB® derivation + multinational TR-DGU® validation, XGBoost comparison, temporal stress test reported.
Limiting factor: AIS-informed construction of the simulated prehospital score, randomized grades for hidden injuries, unclear figure QA, incomplete supplement access.
Would raise: Prospective blinded PHISE collection by EMS with prespecified validation and public analysis code.

Evidence strength
5/10

Rationale: The data support feasibility and retained predictive signal, but not literal equivalence, clinical utility or deployment effectiveness.

Evidence basis: Stand-alone and ML metrics, external-registry results, clinically meaningful outcomes.
Limiting factor: Marked external mortality gap, lower PR performance, no clinical-impact study, source inconsistencies.
Would raise: Prospective field validation with decision-curve / utility analysis and outcome impact.

External validity
6/10

Rationale: US and German-speaking registries provide meaningful geographic diversity, but the external cohort is heavily selected toward severe trauma and university trauma centers.

Evidence basis: >700 NTDB® hospitals and eight European university trauma centers.
Limiting factor: Different registry structures, outcome definitions and prehospital score implementation; 54.4% ISS>15 externally.
Would raise: Validation in routine EMS populations, community/non-academic systems and prospective multi-agency deployment.

Implementation value
5/10

Rationale: The score definition is simple and could be encoded easily, but operational requirements are largely untested.

Evidence basis: Explicit regions/severity mapping, low-complexity aggregation, ML feature integration.
Limiting factor: No interrater reliability, workflow timing, UI, training burden, failure/escalation logic, prospective clinical impact or public code package.
Would raise: EMS implementation protocol, reliability study, open code, prospective safety/utility evaluation.

Major strengths

  • Large derivation cohort and a geographically distinct external registry.
  • Uses both ROC and precision-recall analyses rather than relying on ROC alone.
  • Explicit calibration analysis and SHAP feature interpretation.
  • Targets a real information-timing problem: anatomical severity before CT.
  • Authors appropriately state PHISE is an anatomical component, not a comprehensive risk score.

Major limitations / failure modes

  • Synthetic derivation: definitive AIS injury descriptions are used to construct the simulated prehospital score.
  • Randomized hidden-injury severity: imaging-dependent / undetermined injuries are assigned random grades, making results dependent on simulation assumptions.
  • External instrument mismatch: TR-DGU® records a compatible simplified prehospital injury score, not necessarily the exact PHISE implementation.
  • Operational validity absent: no prospective examiner reliability, time burden, workflow integration or clinical impact.
  • Outcome-definition heterogeneity: NTDB® transfusion is described as packed RBC within 4 h; TR-DGU® is described elsewhere as ED/OR transfusion and in the Outcomes section as RBC within 24 h.
  • Reporting inconsistencies: Figure 4 mortality ROC legend conflicts with results text; Figure 5D uses a transfusion-probability axis despite being captioned mortality calibration; Table 1 outcome percentages lack transparent denominators; NTDB® age IQR differs between prose and table.
  • Reproducibility: code is available only on request; key prompt/hyperparameter details are in unavailable supplementary material; the LLM is called GPT-4o-mini in Results but “GPT-4” in Methods.
  • Title inflation: “matches” is stronger than the reported PR/AUC/calibration results support without an equivalence framework.

AI/ML-specific appraisal

TaskMortality and RBCC transfusion prediction using a prehospital anatomical score plus physiology/mechanism variables.
Data / splitsNTDB® 2019 derivation; 80/20 split with nested/10-fold CV described; later analysis states NTDB® training and TR-DGU® testing.
BaselinesISS, NISS; supplementary comparison with RISC2, TASH, TRISS, rSIG.
MetricsROC AUC, PR AUC, calibration/Brier, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, F1; SHAP importance.
Leakage / optimism riskNot conventional train/test leakage, but the derivation score is built from definitive AIS-coded injury identity, which can make the simulated “prehospital” construct more informed than a real field assessment.
AblationsSeverity-input comparisons are informative; no extensive ablation of individual PHISE components is visible in the main paper.
ReproducibilityPartial. Software versions are reported; code and data require request/purchase/approval; prompt and detailed metrics are supplementary.
Deployment readinessLow. No prospective workflow, reliability, latency, monitoring, human-factors, safety or impact evaluation.

Implementation / practice takeaways

Build-useful
Represent anatomy as a compact structured feature.

A coarse, region-based severity vector can be a useful input alongside physiology without requiring definitive imaging-based scores.

Evaluation-useful
Use PR metrics and calibration, not ROC alone.

Figure 5 looks “close” on ROC while the precision-recall gap is considerably larger; class imbalance makes this distinction important.

Validation-useful
Separate simulated construct validation from field measurement validity.

A score generated from definitive coded diagnoses is not equivalent to a score produced by clinicians under real scene uncertainty.

Do not overclaim
Do not treat PHISE as equivalent to ISS/NISS.

The main paper does not demonstrate formal equivalence/noninferiority and retains meaningful gaps in mortality and PR performance.

Prospective next step
Measure reliability and decision utility.

Needed: interrater agreement, completion time, missingness, occult-injury failure patterns, destination/activation decisions, net benefit and safety.

Practice status
Research / prototype only.

Nothing in the paper supports substituting PHISE for established trauma assessment, imaging, clinical judgment or local triage protocols.
